summary:
Fire Parallax is an interactive, sensor-aware analysis platform that explores how MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations represent burning activity differently across Punjab and Haryana, India. Using NASA FIRMS active-fire data from October–November 2022, the project processes MODIS Aqua and VIIRS NOAA-20 detections and organizes them into a weekly activity calendar.

Users can explore sensor-specific activity, compare spatial co-detections, examine confidence categories, and investigate how results change with different spatial grid sizes and temporal matching windows. The platform makes sensor differences visible while explaining the limitations of interpreting satellite detections.

Fire Parallax addresses the challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspots by providing a transparent, interactive way to compare observations without treating every detection as a unique fire or assuming that differences indicate missed fires.
details:
What does Fire Parallax do?

Fire Parallax is an interactive satellite-data analysis platform that compares MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations over Punjab and Haryana, India. It helps users explore how two satellite sensor systems represent seasonal burning activity differently through weekly calendars, spatial comparisons, confidence categories, and sensitivity analysis.

How does it work?

The project uses NASA FIRMS active-fire observations from October–November 2022. We select MODIS Aqua and VIIRS NOAA-20 detections classified as presumed vegetation fires and preprocess the datasets through validation, coordinate projection, and regional filtering.

The observations are organized into spatial grid cells and UTC dates. When both sensors report at least one qualifying detection in the same state, grid cell, and date, we classify that cell-day as a co-detection. We also examine sensor-specific detections, confidence categories, temporal matching windows, and different grid resolutions (1 km, 2 km, and 5 km).

The results are presented through a seven-section interactive dashboard, allowing users to explore patterns and investigate where the two sensors agree or differ.

What are its benefits and intended impact?

Fire Parallax makes satellite active-fire observations easier to compare and interpret. It helps users understand how sensor characteristics, confidence classifications, spatial resolution, and temporal matching choices influence the patterns they observe.

The intended impact is to encourage more informed interpretation of satellite-based fire monitoring data and demonstrate why observations from different sensors should be compared carefully rather than treated as identical measurements.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using Python, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely, and pyproj for data processing and spatial analysis. Streamlit and Plotly were used to build the interactive dashboard and visualizations. Git and GitHub were used for version control and collaboration.

The project uses satellite observations from NASA FIRMS and administrative boundary data from geoBoundaries. OpenStreetMap and CARTO provide map basemap services. No specialized hardware was required.

What makes the project creative?

Instead of simply displaying hotspot counts, Fire Parallax investigates how the apparent picture of burning activity changes depending on the observing sensor and analytical choices. Its combination of weekly activity calendars, spatial co-detection analysis, confidence exploration, temporal tolerance, and grid-resolution sensitivity gives users multiple ways to investigate sensor disagreement.

It also makes methodological limitations visible, helping users distinguish satellite detections from confirmed physical fire events.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered differences in the MODIS and VIIRS confidence systems, sensor selection, geographic boundaries, UTC acquisition dates, spatial grid resolution, temporal matching tolerance, and grid-origin sensitivity.

We also considered the limitations of the study period and administrative boundary data. The analysis is a two-month, single-year case study, not a multi-year trend analysis.

Importantly, FIRMS detections are thermal observations. They do not independently establish unique physical fires, burned area, or confirmed agricultural burning. Our results are therefore presented as sensor-observation comparisons rather than verified fire-event measurements.
